Keywords: THE, FIRST, FUNERAL

outputs.L1:
**I. – THE FIRST FUNERAL**  
*(The first corpse I saw was on the German wires, and could not be buried)*

The whole field reeked so terribly;  
We smelled the poor dog first:  
His dreadful, swollen belly  
Looked as though it might burst.  

His fur was very untidy;  
He no longer had any eyes.  
It happened on Good Friday,  
And there were swarms of flies.  

Then I felt the coldest  
I had ever felt, and sick;  
But Rose, because she was the oldest,  
Dared to poke him with her stick.  

He felt quite soft and horrible;  
The flies buzzed round his head  
And settled on his forehead.  
Rose whispered, “That dog is dead.”  

“You bury all dead people,  
When they are truly dead,  
Around churches with a steeple:  
Let us bury this,” Rose said.  

“And let us put mint all around it  
To hide the nasty smell.”  
I went to look and found it—  
Plenty, growing near the well.  

We pushed him through the clover  
Into a hole, and then  
We threw brown earth over him  
And said, “Poor dog, Amen.”
outputs.L2:
**I. – THE FIRST BURIAL**  
*(The first dead body I ever saw lay caught on the German barbed wire, where no one could bury it.)*

The entire meadow reeked terribly.  
Before anything else, we noticed the smell of the poor dog.  
His dreadful, puffed-up stomach  
seemed as though it might split open.  

His coat was filthy and disordered,  
and his eyes were gone.  
It was Good Friday when we found him,  
with flies everywhere around.  

Then I became colder than I had ever been,  
and I felt ill.  
But Rose, being the eldest,  
was brave enough to prod him with her stick.  

His body gave way in a horrible, soft way.  
The flies droned around his head  
and landed on his brow.  
Rose said quietly, “That dog is dead.”  

“You’re supposed to bury everyone who has died,  
once they are truly dead,  
in the ground near churches with steeples.  
So we should bury him,” Rose said.  

“And we should scatter mint around him  
to cover up the awful odor.”  
I went searching and discovered some—  
plenty of it, growing by the well.  

We pushed him through the clover  
and into a hollow in the ground.  
Then we covered him completely with dark soil  
and said, “Poor dog, Amen.”
outputs.L3:
On Good Friday, the speaker remembers coming across a dead dog in a field. The place smelled terrible, and the dog’s body was swollen and beginning to decay. Flies covered it, moving over its fur and wounds, and the sight made the speaker feel cold, frightened, and sick.

Among the children, Rose, the oldest, showed the most courage. While the others kept their distance, she took a stick and poked the dog’s body. When it did not move, she told them that it was definitely dead. Her action made the reality of the situation clear to everyone.

The children felt that the dog should not simply be left there to rot. They decided it deserved to be buried properly, almost as if it were a person. Since it was Good Friday, and because they associated burial with church and prayer, they thought the dog should be laid to rest near a holy place.

To make the burial more bearable, they placed mint nearby to cover the smell of decay. Then they dug a hole and put the dog’s body into it. After covering it with earth, they said a simple prayer over the grave. In this way, the children turned a disturbing discovery into a small, solemn act of respect.
outputs.L4:
The children found the dog at the far end of the field, where the grass grew high and dry around the broken fence. They had gone there looking for blackberries, carrying a dented tin pail and a stick for pushing aside nettles, but they stopped as soon as they saw the shape lying half in the weeds.

At first none of them said anything. The dog was on its side, stiff and ruined by the weather, its fur clotted with dirt and burrs. Flies moved over it in a restless cloud, and there was a smell that made the youngest child cover her mouth with both hands. The others stepped back, frightened not only by the dead animal itself but by the strange fact of it being there, so still and abandoned in the bright afternoon.

“Don’t touch it,” one of the boys said.

“I wasn’t going to,” another answered, though he had already picked up a long branch.

They stood in a half-circle, staring. Only a few days earlier, they had seen the same dog running along the road near the farm, thin and dusty, but alive. It had barked at them once and then wagged its tail as if unsure whether to be angry or friendly. Now it seemed impossible that this twisted, silent thing could have been that same creature.

The youngest began to cry, not loudly, but with small, uneven breaths. “We can’t just leave him,” she said.

The others looked at one another. Leaving the dog there suddenly seemed wrong. Until that moment, they had felt only fear and disgust, but her words changed the dead animal into something that had once lived, something that had run, barked, eaten, and maybe belonged to somebody. The field no longer felt like a place for games. It felt like a place where something serious had happened.

“There’s a hole over there,” the oldest boy said.

Near the fence was a shallow pit where rain had washed the earth away. It was not deep, but it was large enough. The children did not want to touch the dog with their hands, so they used sticks and an old board they found nearby. It was difficult work. They pushed and lifted, gagging sometimes and turning their faces away, but they kept at it. The task made them solemn. No one laughed or teased. Even the smallest child helped by pulling weeds from the edge of the hole.

At last they managed to move the dog into the pit. It lay there awkwardly, no longer frightening in the same way. Once it was in the ground, it seemed less like a horrible discovery and more like a body that needed to be cared for.

They began to cover it with earth. They used their hands then, scooping loose soil and dropping it gently over the dog. The dirt fell softly at first, then in heavier handfuls. Someone found a flat stone and placed it at one end of the mound. Another child stuck a few wildflowers into the ground beside it: clover, buttercups, and one crushed daisy from the bottom of the pail.

When the grave was covered, they stood around it quietly. They had all seen funerals before, or at least parts of them—adults in dark clothes, heads bowed, voices lowered, words spoken over a coffin. The children did not know exactly what should be said, but they understood that something had to be said.

The oldest boy took off his cap. The others copied him, though not all of them were wearing hats. They bowed their heads.

“Dear God,” he began, uncertainly. “Please take care of this dog. He didn’t have anybody here, so we buried him. Please let him go to heaven, if dogs go there. Amen.”

“Amen,” the others whispered.

For a moment they remained still. The wind moved through the grass, and the flies, no longer gathered on the body, drifted away in the sunlight. The field became ordinary again, but not quite as it had been before.

Then one of the children picked up the blackberry pail, and they started back toward the road. They walked more slowly than they had come, glancing once or twice over their shoulders at the small mound by the fence.

They did not speak much on the way home. Each of them was thinking, in a child’s way, about death—about how something living could become still, how a body could be frightening and pitiful at the same time, and how the grown-up customs they had seen from a distance might help when no one knew what else to do. By burying the dog, they had made the terrible thing less terrible. They had turned fear into duty, disgust into tenderness, and confusion into a simple act of mercy.
outputs.L5:
**The First Funeral**

The first funeral was a quiet and solemn moment in human history. It marked the first time people gathered not only to say goodbye to someone they loved, but also to show respect, grief, and remembrance. Before words were written and traditions were formed, early humans began to understand the meaning of loss.

A funeral is more than a ceremony. It is a way for the living to honor the dead and comfort one another. The first funeral may have been simple: a body placed carefully in the earth, surrounded by stones, flowers, tools, or personal objects. These gestures showed that the person had mattered in life and would not be forgotten in death.

The first funeral also revealed something deeply human: the ability to feel love, sadness, and hope. It showed that people believed life had meaning beyond the moment. From that first act of farewell grew many customs and rituals that continue across cultures today.

Even now, every funeral carries the same purpose as the first one: to remember, to grieve, and to say a final goodbye with dignity.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem in the style of a WWI-era English poet, titled “The First Funeral,” narrated by a child who finds and buries a dead dog.
counterfactuals.output:
# The First Funeral

I found him where the nettles grew,  
Beside the broken wall,  
With burrs upon his muddy coat  
And flies that did not fall.  

His eyes were open to the sky,  
But would not look at me;  
I called his name, the way I did,  
And waited patiently.  

The lane was quiet after rain,  
The fields were pale and wide;  
A cart went creaking far away,  
And no one came outside.  

I fetched my father’s garden spade—  
It felt too large to hold—  
And dug beneath the apple tree,  
In earth all black and cold.  

The worms were white as candle-wax,  
The roots like fingers lay;  
I did not cry, but bit my sleeve  
And pushed the stones away.  

I made his bed with leaves and grass,  
And set him gently down;  
His paws were stiff, his velvet ears  
Were darker now than brown.  

I said the prayer I half-remembered,  
The one for souls at rest;  
But stopped, because I did not know  
If dogs in Heaven are blessed.  

So then I told him he was good,  
And brave, and quick, and kind—  
The best at chasing rooks away,  
The first a ball to find.  

I covered up his little ribs,  
His collar, and his head;  
The earth fell softly, thud by thud,  
Upon the quiet dead.  

And when the grave was smooth and small,  
I laid a daisy there;  
The wind went by the apple leaves  
As if it said a prayer.  

That night I heard the grown men talk  
Of war beyond the sea,  
Of sons who slept in foreign fields  
As still as he would be.  

I did not understand their words,  
But in my bed I knew  
How deep a hole the heart can dig,  
And what the earth can do.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Can you provide a rhyming poem about children discovering a dead dog on Good Friday and burying it with mint to hide the smell?
counterfactuals.output:
On Good Friday, soft and gray,  
The children found him by the way,  
A little dog beneath the thorn,  
As still as dusk, as cold as morn.  

They fetched a spade, they fetched a sheet,  
And mint from where the garden’s sweet;  
With solemn hands and whispered prayer,  
They made a quiet graveyard there.  

They laid him down below the hill,  
Where springtime rain would find him still,  
And tucked green mint around his head,  
To keep the bitter scent from spreading.  

No bells were rung, no choir sang,  
But through the field their small voices rang:  
“Sleep well, old friend, beneath the clay,  
The mint will bloom here every May.”

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a darkly innocent children’s-voice poem about a first encounter with death, where the speaker and Rose bury a swollen dead dog and say “Poor dog, Amen!”
counterfactuals.output:
Rose found him under the lilac shade,  
big as a pillow, tight and round,  
with flies like buttons on his eyes  
and no more barking in the ground.  

We did not know where dogs go to,  
or if they get to keep their name.  
Rose said heaven had a yard,  
and I said maybe it’s the same.  

We dug with spoons and one red spade  
beside the place the rainpipe cries.  
The earth was black and full of worms,  
the sun was white and full of eyes.  

His fur came loose like dandelion fluff;  
we tried not breathing through our nose.  
I held the tail and Rose the paws,  
because I was brave, and so was Rose.  

We laid him down and tucked him in  
with leaves and dirt and bits of string.  
Rose made a cross from two bent sticks  
and gave the dog a beetle’s wing.  

Then, soft as secrets, small and grim,  
we folded hands like grown-ups can.  
Rose looked at me. I looked at him.  
“Poor dog, Amen!” we said. Amen.
